newsitem.title: INDIA: Four arrested after fire kills 57 in India cinema.
newsitem.headline: Four arrested after fire kills 57 in India cinema.

text.p: Indian police have arrested four managers of a cinema where 57 people died in a fire, and more people were expected to be detained, a senior official said on Saturday.

Deputy police commissioner Maxwell Perreira said authorities have accused the four managers of the capital's Uphaar Grand cinema of criminal negligence in the fire which broke out in the packed movie theatre on Friday.
"We have arrested four people from the cinema's management," Perreira told Reuters. "More arrests are likely."

He said police had registered cases against the four for criminal negligence causing grievous hurt, causing deaths due to criminal negligence and use of combustible materials. The four were to be arraigned in a Delhi court on Saturday.

Perreira said a small fire had broken out on Friday morning in an electrical transformer which hours later exploded in flames during the premiere of the new Hindi movie "Border", which dramatises a 1971 battle between India and Pakistan.
"We will have to see to what extent the transformer was repaired," the police official said.
Most of the victims were trapped in the balcony and suffocated when poisonous smoke engulfed the theatre, which was packed to its capacity of 1,050 seats, Perreira said.
He said the death toll, which late on Friday had been set at 58, had been revised down to 57. A police spokesman said 91 people were injured.
The transformer, located in the basement of the 24-year-old cinema in an affluent South Delhi neighbourhood, caught fire in late Friday afternoon, Perreira said.
"It generated tremendous heat in the entire cable system and the sound-proofing in the walls, which had combustible material, began to smoulder," he said.
"Smoke began collecting in any available space, and by the time the fire broke out, all the escape routes were blocked."
Witnesses described horrific scenes. "I saw women with children in their arms breaking windows and jumping out. It was unbelievable," said one.
"People in the balcony tried to rush into the toilets. The doors to the exits first would not open, and when they did, billowing smoke poured through," Perreira said.
Fire service authorities had recently inspected the cinema and certified that it satisfied safety regulations, Perreira said.

The management of the movie theatre said the transformer belonged to the city's electricity board, Perreira said. The four people who were arrested were in police custody and could not be reached for comment.
Newspapers said the disaster raised questions about respect for safety regulations. "How many of Delhi's cinema halls are following the rules?" the Times of India said.

"If there is one cautionary tale in Friday's tragedy, it is this: our contempt for authorities...is outweighed by our own callousness, our blatant disregard for basic norms of safety or plain civic sense," the Indian Express said in a front-page editorial.
